title: Single-feature linear regression
description: Three points, signed residuals and the lecture's half-MSE cost.
source: Lecture 1 - Introduction.pdf, pages 33 and 36 (PDF page numbers).

pages.title: A line makes a numerical prediction
pages.subtitle: Our goal: measure how well one chosen line fits three observed points.
blocks: Data: (x, y) = (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5). x is an input; y is its known target.
h is the prediction. Theta names the model parameters: theta 0 is the intercept (bias); theta 1 is the slope (weight).
m counts examples. One shared line predicts all three points. These starting parameters are chosen for this study example.

pages.title: Predict all three targets
pages.subtitle: Substitute each input into the same line. Do not change the parameters.
blocks: The superscript (i) identifies an example; it is not an exponent.
Predictions (1, 2, 3) differ from targets (2, 3, 5). Now measure the gaps.

pages.title: Keep the sign, then square
pages.subtitle: Residual means prediction minus target. A negative residual is an underprediction.
blocks: Squaring makes every contribution nonnegative. A gap twice as large contributes four times as much squared error.
Keep the signed residuals too: the next lesson needs them for gradients.

pages.title: Combine errors into one cost
pages.subtitle: The lecture uses half the mean squared error: be careful with the factor 2.
blocks: Lecture 1, PDF page 36. The summation sign means add all example contributions.
The factor 1/2 keeps the best-fit line the same and simplifies derivatives later. It is a convention, not part of every definition of MSE.
A smaller J means a closer fit under this squared-error measure.

pages.title: Picture what the cost measures
pages.subtitle: The vertical gaps are target minus prediction; our signed residual is the reverse.
blocks: All three predictions lie below their targets. Squaring the gaps loses their direction; cost alone does not tell us how to move the line.

pages.title: Your turn: shift the line upward
pages.subtitle: Stop here and calculate before looking at the answer page.
blocks: Use the same three pairs: (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5). Change only the intercept.
1. Calculate all three predictions.
2. Calculate each residual: prediction minus target.
3. Square the residuals and add them.
4. Divide by 2m. Is this cost lower than the original J = 1?
This is a new candidate line, not a gradient-descent update yet.

pages.title: Practice answer and common mistakes
pages.subtitle: Compare each intermediate result with your working.
blocks: This candidate fits better overall. It predicts the first two targets exactly and underpredicts the third by 1.
Common mistakes: dividing by 3 instead of 6; treating (-1)^2 as -1; using a target as the model prediction.
Next: calculate gradients to choose a useful parameter change automatically.
